analysis.one_liner: Makes police departments financially liable when their officers violate constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have made employers of police officers pay for constitutional violations by their officers, never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal civil rights law so that the government employer of a police officer — a city, county, or state agency — is financially liable, like any private employer, when that officer violates someone's constitutional rights on the job. It would also stop employers from hiding behind the officer's personal legal immunity to escape paying. Every American harmed by police misconduct could then recover damages from the department itself, not just from the individual officer.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of police misconduct and their families would gain a realistic path to compensation, because departments and municipalities have far deeper pockets than individual officers and could no longer argue that the officer alone is personally immune. Taxpayers would ultimately benefit too, since departments facing real financial consequences have an incentive to train, supervise, and discipline officers before harms occur.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the employer of a law enforcement officer acting under color of law vicariously liable for the officer's on-the-job acts that deprive people of constitutional rights, in the same way a private employer is liable for negligent employees.

Deems any on-duty officer to be acting within the scope of employment for liability purposes, even when the specific act was unconstitutional, closing a common escape route employers use to deny responsibility.

Prohibits an employer from using the officer's personal immunity as a defense against the vicarious liability claim, so victims could collect from the department even if the officer himself was shielded.
Does not limit or reduce any other legal theories of recovery, so existing avenues of relief against officers or their employers stay open.

analysis.who_pays: Police departments and the cities, counties, and states that employ officers would pay damages in civil rights lawsuits, and those costs would flow through to local taxpayers and municipal liability insurance premiums. Departments would also face the cost of stronger supervision, training, and discipline to limit their new exposure.

drawbacks.text: The costs would land on city and county budgets, meaning local taxpayers — including in departments with generally good records — would ultimately fund the damages and higher insurance premiums.

The bill deems every on-duty officer to be acting within the scope of employment even when the act was unconstitutional, which is broader than ordinary employer-liability rules and would expose governments to suits over conduct they never sanctioned.
No committee hearing, fiscal cost estimate, or witness testimony ever examined the bill's likely price tag or effects on police hiring and recruitment, so its real-world costs are unassessed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people harmed by police misconduct, the benefit is direct and substantial: a legally responsible, financially capable defendant in the police department itself, instead of an often judgment-proof individual officer. The honest cost is that liability would fall on municipal budgets and taxpayers, and the bill's one-size-fits-all 'always in scope' rule goes further than ordinary employment law would. Whether that cost is justified depends on how much financial pressure changes department behavior — an argument the bill never got the chance to make, because it received no hearing or debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on July 29, 2020, during the national debate over police accountability that followed George Floyd's killing.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, whose approval is the first step for any civil rights law change.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors, including none of the other 230 House Democrats.
The Judiciary Committee never held a markup or scheduled the bill, and it died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments and the municipal governments that employ officers are better off, because they were never exposed to the new vicarious liability the bill would have created, and officers' existing immunities were left untouched.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 29, 2020, proposing employer liability and an immunity bar for civil rights claims against police employers.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup, hearing, or vote; the bill sat until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Democratic Caucus
against.role: Majority party controlling the House and its committee calendar
against.what_they_did: Provided no cosponsors — not one of the chamber's other 230 Democrats signed on — leaving the bill with no coalition to push it onto the agenda.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only partisan signal is that the bill's single supporter was a Democrat and none of the other 230 House Democrats or 197 Republicans cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies and their municipal employers
industries.note: The bill would have made departments and the cities and counties behind them pay damages when officers violate constitutional rights, replacing today's system where individual officers' immunities usually leave victims with no collectable defendant. Its death preserves the status quo in which the agencies that control training and discipline face no direct financial consequence.
Broader employer liability for police misconduct would have meant more claims and higher premiums, but also a larger market for municipal coverage. The bill's failure leaves this market unchanged.
